title: How can I better understand the poetry of Wings of Desire?

commenti.body:
I wish I had the ability to do a better job or more thorough write up than this, but this is my first post for film analysis I've ever done.  Be gentle.

I think that the dichotomy of space, fantasy and reality (circus performers and actors), English and German, music (classical and modern) are purposeful in their inability to reflect the full truth.  

I felt a need to comment because this is one of my favorite films in its complete sincerity and inability to ever properly conclude itself.  Being left to the whim of a translator is in itself a reflection, and the transition from English to German and back only builds that mystery.

I really love [this](https://reverseshot.org/symposiums/entry/3106/wings_of_desire#:~:text=Wings%20of%20Desire%20argues%20for,of%20a%20man%20and%20woman) article if you want a deeper scholastic view, but I just adore how this film make you reach for a world you can never touch without leaving your own.

I can't guarantee the accuracy but this site claims to be a transcript:  [https://transcripts.foreverdreaming.org/viewtopic.php?t=39967&sid=f6bf6371d1b5ffc883a3846baedd3ebc&view=print](https://transcripts.foreverdreaming.org/viewtopic.php?t=39967&sid=f6bf6371d1b5ffc883a3846baedd3ebc&view=print)
Thank you for your comment and the link.

I don't know which translation you're seeing, but it's probably accurate. The language of the poem(s) by Peter Handke is simple and child-like, because it's from the perspective of a child thinking big thoughts and asking big questions for the first time, marveling at its own existence. 

That said, you probably have a few years left in your life (if not decades) - why not learn German?
Now that you put it like that, maybe I should.
